01 · Executive Summary

July delivered strong revenue at ₹24.54L net — above the 2026 Avg (excl. Jul) average, with declining trial conversion and stabilising churn as the key watchpoints.

Headline revenue closed at ₹24.54L net (₹25.80L gross, ₹1.70L discount), which is +18.2% vs Jun 2026 (M-1), +6.2% vs May 2026 (M-2), +5.9% vs 2026 Avg (excl. Jul), and +37.1% vs Jul 2025 (YoY). Trial conversion is 28.9% (35 of 121 trials), down -2.2pp MoM. Churn rate stands at 22.5%, improving -11.2pp MoM. Discount efficiency is ₹15.19 of revenue collected per ₹1 discounted.

Executive Strategic Analysis — July 2026
Strategic Analysis & Action Plan

July’s revenue momentum is healthy; the management question is whether conversion and retention quality can keep pace with that growth.

💡 What the Numbers Mean — in Plain English (5)
  • 💡
    Revenue Growth Driven by Volume
    The studio achieved an impressive revenue growth of 18.3%, primarily due to a significant increase in transactions (+23.8%). This indicates strong market pull and effective customer acquisition strategies. (₹25,80,029 gross (+18.3%) driven by 349 transactions (+23.8%), while ATV decreased by -4.4%)
  • 💡
    Opportunity in Lead Conversion
    Lead-to-trial conversion stands at 26.6%, below industry benchmarks of 30-45%. Improving this metric can double the pipeline without additional marketing spend. (Lead conversion rate is at 26.6% compared to previous month's rate of 24.2%)
  • 💡
    Check-in Frequency Indicates Engagement Gap
    Average check-ins per member are at 3.7, suggesting that while members are visiting, there is potential to increase engagement closer to the industry standard of 8-12 visits/month. ('Check-ins per member' stands at 3.7 against benchmarks of active members visiting 8-12x/month.)
  • 💡
    Churn Rate Signals Retention Opportunity
    'Hard churn' rate is notably high at 22.5%, providing an opportunity for targeted retention initiatives that could stabilize membership numbers and improve net member change. ('Hard churn' rate is currently at 22.5% with net member flow showing -120.)
  • 💡
    'Top Trainer' Dependency Risk Identified
    'Top trainer concentration' risk exists as top trainers handle over half the sessions, which could impact service quality if any one trainer becomes unavailable. ('Top three trainers account for over half (54%) of session visits')

Key Insights · July 2026
01
Revenue at ₹24.54L net (+5.9% vs 2026 Avg (excl. Jul)) — Volume-Driven Lift.
Net sales sit at ₹24.54L (+5.9% vs 2026 Avg (excl. Jul) average of ₹23.18L, +18.2% vs Jun 2026). Transactions (349) and ATV (₹7,393) reveal the growth engine.
What this tells us: Top-line momentum is active, but discounting (6.6% penetration) is eroding margin yield.
Strategic Action: Pivot from price discounting to value-add bonuses to stabilize ATV and recover ~₹1.1L/mo in net margin.
02
Trial conversion rate at 28.9% (+8.4pp vs 2026 Avg (excl. Jul)) — Strong Conversion.
35 of 121 trialists converted (28.9%), -2.2pp vs Jun 2026 and 2026 Avg (excl. Jul) average of 20.5%.
What this tells us: The trial experience is effectively convincing prospects to join.
Strategic Action: Expand lead acquisition spend on high-converting channels.
03
Churn at 22.5% (+0.6pp vs 2026 Avg (excl. Jul)) — Retention Leakage.
Of 120 expiring memberships, 83 renewed (69.2%), while 27 lapsed (22.5% churn).
What this tells us: Lapses are escalating among members with declining check-in frequency in month 3.
Strategic Action: Set automated alerts when a member visits fewer than 3 times in 30 days to trigger coach check-ins.
04
Discount Efficiency at ₹15.19 per ₹1 Discounted — Margin Healthy.
Discounts total ₹1.70L against ₹25.80L gross (6.6% penetration) vs 2026 Avg (excl. Jul) efficiency of ₹7.28.
What this tells us: Promotional offers are yielding adequate net sales return.
Strategic Action: Maintain current pricing controls.
05
Fill Rate at 47.3% across 368 Sessions — Utilization Signal.
368 sessions generated 2,432 visits (avg 6.6/session), +1.0pp vs Jun 2026 vs 2026 Avg (excl. Jul) average of 44.5%.
What this tells us: Prime slots are running near capacity while off-peak hours pull down overall facility utilization.
Strategic Action: Reallocate low-fill off-peak hours to peak class formats to unlock ~40 incremental visits per week.
06
Lead Volume at 154 Leads (+7.3% vs 2026 Avg (excl. Jul)) — Pipeline Health.
Lead volume sits +20.3% vs Jun 2026 vs 2026 Avg (excl. Jul) average of 144. Top source: Hosted Class (37 leads, 2 converted).
What this tells us: Lead acquisition is generating steady prospect volume.
Strategic Action: Scale ad spend on top-performing acquisition channels.
07
295 Late Cancels (4 Heavy Cancelers) — Capacity Loss.
Late-cancel rate is 10.8% of check-ins (+0.7pp vs Jun 2026), with 4 members canceling 5+ times. Zero penalty collected.
What this tells us: Unenforced cancellation policies result in wasted spot capacity and prevent waitlisted members from attending.
Strategic Action: Implement a standard ₹250 late-cancel fee to recover lost spots and improve class commitment.
08
Flagship anchor: 46.4% of group sales — an outsized contribution.
Kwality House delivered ₹25.80L of the group’s ₹55.58L July gross — comfortably ahead of Bandra (₹18.89L) and Kenkere House (₹10.88L) on a base of 239 active clients.
What this tells us: The Barre + Cycle + Strength diversification and premium South Mumbai positioning is the group’s proven growth playbook.
Strategic Action: Protect the flagship — every fix below (trial retention, instructor mix, discount leakage) carries group-level revenue implications.
09
The April anniversary hangover has cleared — organic demand is back.
April’s anniversary campaign spiked sales to ~₹50.0L, then May fell -51.5% and June -10.2% as clients burned pre-bought packages. July’s +18.3% MoM rebound marks a return to organic run-rate.
What this tells us: Current growth is no longer propped up by campaign pull-forward.
Strategic Action: Treat ₹24–26L as the clean demand floor for August targets; space mega-promos at least two quarters apart to avoid recycling the hangover.
10
Returning members are the engine: 83.1% of July sales.
Returning clients contributed ₹21.44L (+34.8% YoY, +31.5% MoM), and average spend per returning client rose to ₹13,833 (+23.0% MoM).
What this tells us: The loyal base is deepening — upsell and renewal journeys work when the relationship exists.
Strategic Action: Keep renewal upgrades and annual conversions at the centre of the August plan; this cohort already outspends newcomers 2.7×.
11
New-customer spend collapsed to ₹5,189 (-31.4% YoY) — zero unlimited memberships sold to newcomers.
84 new buyers came in (+12.0% MoM) yet contributed only ₹4.36L (-20.8% MoM): 29 bought single classes, 17 the 2-for-1 special, 4 the two-week trial — none bought a 1/3/12-month unlimited membership. Expected LTV of July’s new clients fell to ₹7,889 (-74% YoY).
What this tells us: Acquisition volume is healthy; first-purchase upgrade is the broken link.
Strategic Action: Move the desk offer from ‘come back’ to bundle-first (8/12-class or 1-month) within 72 hours of trial.

The July balance sheet — what worked vs. what didn’t

A two-column read of the month, drawn from the sales, session, funnel, churn and instructor deep dives. Wins to protect on the left; leaks to fix in August on the right.

What worked in July
✓
Renewal & churn momentum regained
69.2% of July expirations renewed (+4.7pp MoM) and churn improved from 33.7% to 22.5%. Pre-expiry outreach is working — maintain the cadence.
✓
Price rises absorbed without demand loss
Average membership prices rose across the board — 1-Month +5.8% (₹18,389), 3-Month +21.2% (₹51,677), Annual +6.0% (₹165,069) — yet membership revenue still grew +4.5% YoY. Clear evidence of premium pricing power.
✓
Strength Lab & Express formats are capacity-constrained hits
Full Body 89.0%, Push 83.0%, Pull 79.8% and PowerCycle Express 88.0% fill — demand now exceeds supply, the highest-margin scheduling problem a studio can have.
✓
Leanest cost month of the year
Discounts held at 6.5% of gross and 85.8% of sales ran on zero-fee channels (Custom / Cash), saving ~₹62K in processor fees versus a card-heavy mix.
What needs attention
✗
The post-trial exodus
74% of first-time trialers never returned: trial retention collapsed to 28.9% vs 53.9% a year ago. The studio pays for acquisition it doesn’t keep.
✗
New-buyer value collapse
New customer average spend fell to ₹5,189 (-31.4% YoY); 53% of converted trialers bought only a single class and expected LTV dropped -74% YoY.
✗
Hosted & celebration formats drain prime slots
37 hosted-class leads produced just 2 conversions (5.4%); hosted celebration formats convert at 0–12.5% vs 31% for Studio Barre 57.
✗
Compliance & data exposure
Applied GST moved 18% → 5% (collections -61.7% YoY), 47.8% of POS rows carry a placeholder transaction ID, and 350 CRM leads marked ‘Membership Sold’ show ₹0 LTV.

Memberships carry 47% of revenue, with healthy category diversification across the portfolio, and the studio’s payment mix is diverse at 4 methods.

Revenue Quality & Monetization Analysis — July 2026
Composition, pricing power & margin leaks
📋 Detailed Revenue Narrative

July’s ₹24.54L net is genuine growth, but its quality is mixed. The studio shook off the April anniversary hangover (₹50.0L peak → ₹24.3L in May → ₹21.8L in June) on the back of record transactions (349, +23.8% MoM), while ATV slid to ₹7,393 (-4.4% MoM, -22% vs the H1 average of ₹9,538) because single classes (+52.1% YoY) and newcomer specials grew fastest. Memberships surged +44.3% MoM to ₹12.17L — powered by price rises (3-Month +21.2%, Annual +6.0%) rather than volume (-26.2% units YoY) — and three annual closes alone delivered 19.2% of the month. Payment discipline (85.8% fee-free channels, ~₹62K saved) and the leanest discounting of the year (6.5%) protected margin. Two exposures now need board attention: the applied GST rate moved 18% → 5% (collections -61.7% YoY) and 47.8% of POS rows carry a duplicated placeholder transaction ID.

💡 What the Numbers Mean — in Plain English (5)
  • 💡
    Volume-led, value-diluted growth
    349 transactions (+23.8% MoM) delivered the +18.2% revenue lift, but ATV fell to ₹7,393 as the mix tilted toward single classes and newcomer specials. Growth stays healthy only if these low-ticket buyers upgrade. (Single-class revenue +52.1% YoY vs. memberships +4.5% YoY)
  • 💡
    Price rises are sticking
    Membership average prices rose with no visible demand destruction: 1-Month ₹18,389 (+5.8%), 3-Month ₹51,677 (+21.2%), Annual ₹165,069 (+6.0%). The premium brand carries real pricing power. (Membership revenue +4.5% YoY on -26.2% unit volume)
  • 💡
    Three whale closes = 19.2% of sales
    Three Studio Annual Unlimited memberships (~₹1.65L each) closed by Vahishta Fitter and Akshay Rane generated ₹4.95L of lump-sum cash flow from just three clients. (S. Ghiasi, P. Rathi & K. Nebhnani; lumpy but decisive for beating baseline)
  • 💡
    Payment mix saved ~₹62K in fees
    Only 14.2% of gross ran over Stripe (2.88% processor fee, ₹10.5K); 85.8% used zero-fee Custom / Cash channels. Every +10pp shifted from Stripe to bank transfer saves ~₹7K/mo. (₹62,000 approximate July saving vs a card-heavy mix)
  • 💡
    The ‘Retail’ line is mostly venue hire
    72.5% (₹49.4K) of the ₹68.0K retail line came from studio book-outs; true merchandise sales were ₹18.7K — about ₹78 per active client. The shop programme has failed to attach. (Retail -28.8% YoY despite the space-booking support)

🎯
Pipeline & Conversion Quality Analysis — July 2026
Top of funnel is healthy; conversion quality & CRM hygiene are not
📋 Detailed Funnel Narrative

154 leads (+20.3% MoM, +87.8% YoY) and 121 trials (+59.2% YoY) prove that marketing reach is not the constraint. The constraint is what happens around the trial: of the leads who completed a trial, 43.2% converted, versus under 1% for those who never did — the on-floor experience is genuinely persuasive. Yet the July conversion cohort bought small: average LTV of converted leads collapsed to ₹2,558 (-66% MoM), and only 1 of 32 converted trialers took an unlimited membership. Meanwhile 37 hosted-class leads returned 2 conversions (5.4%), the website produced 25 leads at 12.0%, 29 leads sit parked at ‘Trial Completed’ without follow-up, and 350 CRM records marked ‘Membership Sold’ show ₹0 purchases — overstating pipeline truth and hiding the follow-up queue.

💡 What the Numbers Mean — in Plain English (6)
  • 💡
    The trial is the entire game
    43.2% of trial-completing leads convert; fewer than 1% of non-trialers do. Every process should push one thing: get the lead into a class within 72 hours. (88 trial leads → 38 conversions; non-trial path near zero)
  • 💡
    Hosted Class: volume without value
    37 hosted leads (24% of inflow) returned 2 conversions at single-class value. Co-branded events fill the studio with free-riders while consuming prime slots. (5.4% conversion vs 45.5% for client referrals)
  • 💡
    Website & walk-ins under-convert
    Website leads converted at 12.0% (3 of 25) and walk-ins at 14.3% — weak for high-intent channels. The landing page needs a WhatsApp-direct ‘Book a Trial’ (WhatsApp closes at 41.7%). (Self-guided digital traffic is reaching the desk without a script)
  • 💡
    Conversion value is collapsing
    July’s converted cohort carries an average LTV of just ₹2,558 (-66% MoM, -69% YoY). ‘Converted’ increasingly means a single-class buyer, not a member. (53% of converted trialers bought only a single class; 1 of 32 took unlimited)
  • 💡
    CRM hygiene: 350 ghost ‘sold’ records
    350 leads marked ‘Membership Sold’ have zero purchases and zero LTV — premature stage-flipping or payment-process failures. Another 29 July leads sit stuck at ‘Trial Completed’. (Reconcile stages to POS payments before CRM is board-usable)
  • 💡
    Voice and messaging close best
    Incoming calls converted at 62.5% and WhatsApp enquiries at 41.7% — the two most human channels outperformed every passive one. (Enforce a 24-hour first-call rule and a 48-hour post-trial follow-up)

Delivery, Utilization & Instructor Analysis — July 2026
Diversification is paying; overscheduling the tail is not
📋 Detailed Operations Narrative

The +41% YoY schedule build-out looked like a dilution risk, yet occupancy rose to 47.3% (from 43.5% LY) because average class capacity was deliberately cut from 16.8 to 14.0 seats — smaller rooms, premium pricing, and ₹865 revenue per visit (+17.8% YoY). The 100%-Barre studio of 2025 is now 58% Barre / 25% Cycle / 17% Strength, and Strength Lab (79.8–89.0% fill) plus PowerCycle Express (88.0%) are capacity-constrained rather than demand-constrained. The costs of expansion show up in the tail: 16 sessions ran completely empty (4.35% of the schedule vs 1.53% LY), Cardio Barre variants sit at 23.9–34.2% fill, and an ‘Unknown Class’ mapping bucket is leaking schedule accuracy across 18 sessions. Instructor-wise, Rohan Dahima (8.56 avg class, zero empties, 72.7% new-client retention) and Cauveri Vikrant (41 sessions, 12.2% empty, 11.1% retention) are carrying identical loads with opposite returns.

💡 What the Numbers Mean — in Plain English (6)
  • 💡
    Diversification drove +50.6% session revenue
    From 261 all-Barre classes (Jul 2025) to 368 mixed classes (Jul 2026) — Barre 58.4% / Cycle 24.7% / Strength 16.8% of schedule attracted an entirely new demographic. (Session revenue ₹21.03L, +50.6% YoY, +17.8% MoM)
  • 💡
    Smaller rooms = premium economics
    Average capacity cut -16.7% per class lifted fill +3.8pp and value per visit +17.8% to ₹865 — the premium-service transition is measurably working. (Class size dilution (-9.3% YoY to 6.61) is intentional, not slippage)
  • 💡
    Strength Lab is supply-constrained
    Full Body 89.0%, Push 83.0%, Pull 79.8% and PowerCycle Express 88.0% fill — four formats effectively sell out. Each added Strength session historically yields ~₹3.5–4.0K/session. (Highest-margin scheduling move available for August)
  • 💡
    Empty-class payroll leak doubled down
    16 sessions (4.35%) ran empty, costing instructor payroll with zero attendance — concentrated with Cauveri (5), Karanvir (3) and Simonelle (3). (Three-consecutive-week prune rule removes this permanently)
  • 💡
    Cardio Barre / Recovery tail is dragging fill
    Cardio Barre Express 23.9%, Cardio Barre Plus 26.4%, Recovery 25.0%, Back Body Blaze 26.9% — ~32 classes under 27% fill. (Consolidate into 1–2 flagship slots each; reallocate prime time to Strength / Express)
  • 💡
    Late-cancel discipline improved -8.7pp YoY
    From 19.5% of bookings (Jul 2025) to 10.8% (Jul 2026) — client commitment is improving. The 295 remaining cancels remain an unpaid-capacity leak (see Section 06). (Half the battle is won; a ₹500 fee + 2h reminders finishes it)

💙
Churn Signals & Active-Risk Analysis — July 2026
The historical base is loyal; the current book is fragile
📋 Detailed Retention Narrative

History says Kwality retains: 77.2% of 10,458 known-outcome contracts renewed. But the live book tells a different story — of 208 currently active clients, 71 are flagged high-risk and 30 medium-risk: 48.5% of the active base is in danger of lapsing right now, representing roughly ₹10–14L of monthly spend at stake. The triggers are mechanical, not emotional: lapsed clients averaged 3.04 sessions before drifting (vs 5.38 for renewers), cancelled 14.6% of bookings (vs 8.6%), and hover at 0.8–1.2 visits per week. Risk spikes at the 7th and 21st class milestones. Notably, price is not the problem — discounted contracts renew at 78.7% vs 77.0% for full price — while seller behaviour matters: historic renewal of sold contracts spans 92.8% (Jimmeey Gondaa) to 51.9% (Saniya Makwana), with top revenue-closer Vahishta at 67.6%, indicating some oversized deals are being sold to mismatched clients.

💡 What the Numbers Mean — in Plain English (6)
  • 💡
    48.5% of the active base is at-risk right now
    71 high-risk + 30 medium-risk of 208 active clients. A weekly named-outreach protocol is the difference between a lapsed book that shrinks and one that compounds past 482. (₹10–14L/mo of spend sits with the at-risk pool)
  • 💡
    Under 4 sessions is the cliff edge
    Churners averaged 3.04 completed sessions before lapsing vs 5.38 for renewers. Every new buyer must cross 4 classes inside 14 days or drift sets in. (‘4-in-14’ activation rule; below 1.2 visits/week = flag)
  • 💡
    Cancellations foreshadow the lapse
    Lapsed members cancelled 14.6% of bookings — nearly double the 8.6% of renewers. A cancellation is a retention signal, not an logistics note. (Auto-reschedule WhatsApp within 15 minutes of every cancel)
  • 💡
    Classes 7 and 21 are the wobble milestones
    Risk spikes at scheduling-fatigue points where novelty fades and plateaus appear. Proactive coach check-ins at these exact moments intercept the drift. (Milestone shout-outs + progress note + guest pass at #7 and #21)
  • 💡
    Discounts don’t buy loyalty here
    Discounted contracts renew at 78.7% vs 77.0% for full-price. Kwality’s base is price-inelastic — stop pre-emptive renewal discounts and invest in attendance nudges instead. (₹1.70L of July discounting was largely defensive, not accretive)
  • 💡
    Seller-linked churn is real
    Historic renewal spans 92.8% (Jimmeey, 125 contracts) and 88.4% (Zahur, 86) down to 51.9% (Saniya) and 64.6% (Sheetal). Vahishta’s ₹12.5K-ATV book retains at 67.6% across 339 contracts. (Sell fit, not size — make 90-day retention a seller bonus metric)

Complimentary / referral-free / influencer-free / staff-family classes are also excluded (zero LTV). Strategic Action: Retire pre-emptive renewal discounts; offer value-adds (guest passes, priority booking, private session) instead — they cost margin only when used.

Active risk profile — the 101-client watchlist and its triggers

Retention risk is measurable before it becomes churn: attendance frequency, cancellation rate and class milestones predict lapse with enough lead time to intervene.

Trigger insights
01
The 4-class cliff: churners averaged 3.04 sessions; renewers 5.38.
Any new buyer under 4 completed sessions inside their first fortnight is statistically pre-lapse.
Strategic Action: ‘Quick Starter’ reward — complete 4 classes in 14 days, get a recovery shake + grip socks on the house.
02
Under 1.2 visits per week is the #1 live flag.
High-risk actives average 0.8–1.2 classes/week — frequency dies before the membership does.
Strategic Action: CRM alert at <3 visits in a rolling 30 days → front-desk call within 24 hours.
03
Classes 7 and 21 are the churn inflection points.
Risk spikes at these milestones — novelty fades around #7; routine/plateau fatigue hits at #21.
Strategic Action: Coach shout-out, progress note and a guest pass at each milestone, timed to the exact class count.
04
Cancellations foreshadow the lapse: 14.6% vs 8.6%.
The cancelling member is mid-decision; silence after a cancel consents to the drift.
Strategic Action: Every cancel fires an auto-reschedule WhatsApp within 15 minutes with two named alternative slots.

Consolidated Decision Memo — July 2026
The moves that matter, ranked by leverage
📋 Detailed Memo Narrative

Everything in Sections 1–5 compresses into a short memo. July’s growth is real but thinning in quality: ATV -4.4% MoM, new-buyer expected LTV -74% YoY, and a 74% post-trial exodus. Critically, the highest-leverage fixes are operational rather than expensive — a 48-hour post-trial close protocol, trial slots re-weighted to proven instructor-closers, a hosted-events budget swap into referrals, systematic reactivation of the 482-member lapsed book, and schedule pruning of empty and under-filled classes. And two non-revenue items carry outsized downside and must precede everything else: the GST-rate question (18% → 5%) and the POS/CRM data repairs, both detailed in Section 02 and Section 03.

🎯 Priority Recommendations (6)
  • ✅
    1. Install the 48-hour post-trial close protocol
    No first-time trialer leaves without a 2-minute desk consult; automated SMS/WhatsApp drip fires within 24h with a fast-action bundle offer (10% off an 8/12-class pack or 1-month unlimited + grip socks).
    Expected impact: Lifting trial retention 28.9% → 40% ≈ +13 returning members/mo ≈ ₹1.6–2.3L
  • ✅
    2. Re-slot trials to proven instructor-closers
    Move July’s trial-heavy slots to Pranjali (50% conv), Simonelle (37.5%) and Rohan (66.7% retention); take Cauveri & Reshma off trial duties for 60 days with shadowing; reduce Cauveri’s total load 41 → 25.
    Expected impact: Recovers a quarter of the funnel currently burning at <8% conversion
  • ✅
    3. Swap hosted-event spend for a referral engine
    Cap hosted/celebration events at 1–2 per month with a paid RSVP gate; launch a ₹2,000 member-get-member credit. Referrals convert at 45.5% vs 5.4% for hosted leads.
    Expected impact: Higher-quality pipeline at equal or lower spend
  • ✅
    4. Run the lapsed-book win-back & pre-expiry cadence
    ‘We Miss You’ campaign to the 482-member lapsed pool (15% target ≈ 72 members); 30/60/90-day pre-expiry outreach; ₹250–500 late-cancel fee + 2-hour reminders.
    Expected impact: ~₹14.5L lifetime reactivation pool; ~₹0.7–1.5L/mo from cancel discipline
  • ✅
    5. Repair compliance & data foundations first
    Verify GST 18% → 5% with the CA (indicative exposure ~₹3L+/mo at July volumes if misapplied); fix the POS placeholder-ID bug (47.8% of rows); audit the 350 ghost ‘Membership Sold’ CRM records.
    Expected impact: Removes statutory tail-risk and restores trustworthy reporting
  • ✅
    6. Protect pricing power; stop fighting mix with discounts
    Prices rose 5.8–21.2% without demand loss — the brand has headroom. Discounts don’t lift renewal (78.7% vs 77.0%), so hold the 6.6% cap and fix mix with bundle-first selling instead.
    Expected impact: Recovers ~₹1.1L/mo of margin dilution vs the H1 AOV of ₹9,538

Outlook & Value-at-Stake Analysis — August 2026
What the base case hides, and what each lever is worth
📋 Detailed Outlook Narrative

The base case (₹23.3–24.5L) assumes July’s structure persists: healthy acquisition, soft conversion value, and an unmanaged at-risk book. The risk distribution is asymmetric. Downside items are policy and statutory — a GST reassessment (~₹3L+/mo if 18% applies) and a 101-client at-risk pool carrying roughly ₹10–14L/mo of spend. Upside levers are operational and already proven in-studio: the post-trial close, instructor re-slotting, lapsed reactivation, late-cancel policy and schedule pruning sum to an estimated ₹4.9–7.7L/month — comfortably covering the gap to the ₹27–28.2L August upside case and making the ₹30–34.8L steady state credible by October.

💡 What the Numbers Mean — in Plain English
  • 💡
    Several practical improvements can combine into one meaningful lift
    The upside forecast does not depend on one dramatic bet. Faster follow-up after a trial helps more newcomers return, firmer cancellation rules protect seats that would otherwise go unused, and a smarter timetable places more classes where demand is strongest. Better lead sources bring in more serious prospects, win-back outreach reconnects with former members, and clearer package choices improve the value of each sale. Together, these manageable operational changes make the higher revenue scenario realistic rather than aspirational.
  • 💡
    Protecting existing members matters more than simply buying more leads
    Almost half of the active client base is showing early signs of disengagement, such as attending less often or cancelling more frequently. These members already know and trust the studio, so a personal check-in, a convenient class recommendation, or help restarting their routine can be more valuable than spending more money to attract a stranger. Retention work protects a large share of the studio’s dependable monthly revenue.
  • 💡
    The GST question can materially change how the revenue result should be read
    July’s net revenue looks especially strong partly because the tax rate used in billing appears to have moved from 18% to 5%. If that lower rate is correct, the improvement is valid. If it is not, part of the apparent gain could become tax payable later. Management should therefore obtain written confirmation from the accountant and billing provider before treating the full net-revenue increase as permanent performance.
  • 💡
    A newcomer’s first purchase shows whether the sales conversation is working
    The average first purchase tells us whether new clients are making a meaningful commitment or only testing the studio with the smallest option. If this amount continues to fall, it means the desk team is not clearly connecting a client’s goals to the right package. A healthier result would show more newcomers choosing an eight-class pack, a twelve-class pack, or a one-month membership after their trial.
  • 💡
    Hosted events should earn their place on the calendar
    Hosted classes can create visibility, but July’s attendees rarely became paying members. They also occupied Saturday periods when regular clients tend to make higher-value purchases. Future events should therefore have a clear audience, a paid reservation or qualification step, and a follow-up plan. If an event cannot produce qualified trials or memberships, that time and budget should move to referrals and direct trial bookings.

Value at stake — the August bridge

Indicative monthly levers behind the ₹27–28L upside case and the ₹30–35L steady state. Estimates assume execution from August W2–W3 and are deliberately conservative.

Bridge insights
01
Post-trial recovery is the largest single lever (₹1.6–2.3L/mo).
Moving trial retention from 28.9% to 40% adds ~13 returning members a month (121-trial cohort × ~11pp), at ₹12–17.5K of first-package value each.
What this tells us: Retention work at the desk beats new marketing spend.
02
Retention economics dwarf acquisition economics.
Reactivating 15% of the 482-member lapsed book (~72 members) unlocks a ~₹14.5L lifetime pool (≈ ₹1.2L/mo amortised over 12 months) at near-zero acquisition cost.
What this tells us: The studio has already paid to acquire these members once; the second purchase is almost pure margin.

A · Commercial & Revenue Metrics
MetricHow it is calculatedWhat it tells the business
Net Sales Gross collections minus all discounts; excludes VAT/GST. July: ₹24.54L. The true top-line — the number every growth target references.
Gross Sales Total billed value across all 349 completed transactions, before discounts are netted out. Realised demand / cash through the register.
Transactions Count of completed sale events (349; +23.8% MoM). Volume of buying decisions — July’s growth engine.
Unique Buyers Distinct clients with ≥1 completed transaction (232). Breadth of the buying base, distinct from transaction volume.
ATV / AOV Net Sales ÷ Transactions. July: ₹7,393 (-4.4% MoM, -12.3% YoY; H1 avg ₹9,538). Ticket-size health; single-class-heavy mix drags it down.
Discount Value Σ of all promotional/markdown amounts (₹1.70L). Absolute margin give-away in the month.
Discount Penetration Discount Value ÷ Gross Sales. July: 6.6% vs 13.1% 2026 baseline. Pricing discipline; red-flag threshold at 10%.
Discount Efficiency Net Sales ÷ Discount Value. July: ₹15.19 collected per ₹1 discounted (baseline ₹7.28). Whether discount spend is buying revenue efficiently.
Returning vs New Revenue Split Revenue split by buyer tenure. Returning: ₹21.44L = 83.1% of sales; new: ₹4.36L. Whether growth is loyalty-led or acquisition-led.
Avg Spend — Returning / New Client Segment revenue ÷ segment buyers. Returning ₹13,833 (+23% MoM) vs new ₹5,189 (-31% YoY). Onboarding value gap — newcomers are under-monetised.
Group Revenue Share Studio gross ÷ group gross. July: ₹25.80L ÷ ₹55.58L = 46.4%. Flagship standing vs Bandra (₹18.89L) & Kenkere (₹10.88L).
Revenue per Visit Session-attributed net revenue ÷ checked-in visits. July: ₹21.03L ÷ 2,432 = ₹865 (+17.8% YoY). Monetisation quality of each workout delivered.
Payment Mix / Fee Leakage Gross share by payment method; Stripe carries a 2.88% processor fee. 85.8% fee-free mix saved ~₹62K in July; card mix is a controllable margin leak.
B · Sessions & Utilisation Metrics
MetricHow it is calculatedWhat it tells the business
Sessions Scheduled classes delivered (368; +41.0% YoY). The supply side of the studio.
Visits / Check-ins Attended bookings (2,432; +6.6% MoM, +27.9% YoY). Delivered demand.
Capacity Σ of bookable seats across all sessions. Avg capacity/class cut 16.8 → 14.0 (-16.7%). Smaller rooms drove fill +3.8pp and premium pricing power.
Fill Rate Visits ÷ Capacity. July: 47.3% (+1.0pp MoM). Utilisation of the room; prime slots near-sellout while off-peak lags.
Class Avg Visits ÷ Sessions. July: 6.6 (-9.3% YoY — deliberate smaller rooms). Room energy and per-class economics.
Late Cancels / Late-Cancel Rate Cancellations inside the late window ÷ bookings. July: 295 = 10.8% (vs 19.5% Jul-25). Unpaid capacity waste; fee-policy target with ~₹1.5L/mo at stake.
Empty Session Rate Sessions with zero check-ins ÷ sessions. July: 16 = 4.35% (vs 1.53% Jul-25). Payroll paid to teach empty rooms; prune-rule target.
Unique Attendees Distinct clients attending ≥1 session. Active community breadth, per class-format line.
Slot Heat (heatmap cells) Visits per day-of-week × start-time slot (Sat 11:30 peak = 121). Where to add, move, or cut classes on the weekly grid.

MetricHow it is calculatedWhat it tells the business

Converted Trialists making a first purchase (35; -5.4% MoM). Funnel output for the month.
Conversion Rate (headline) Converted ÷ Trials. July: 35 ÷ 121 = 28.9% (-2.2pp MoM, -14.5pp YoY). Core sales-efficiency KPI; the key watchpoint.
Lead-to-Conversion Rate Leads converted (any source cohort) ÷ leads created. July: 41 ÷ 154 = 26.6%. End-to-end channel quality.
Trial-to-Conversion Rate Converted ÷ leads who completed a trial. July: 38 ÷ 88 = 43.2% (non-trialers: <1%). Proof the trial class is the conversion gateway.
